findings.title: Direct fetch error path throws plain Error instead of ApiError
findings.rationale: The new `downloadFindingsCsv` helper calls `fetch` directly and, on a non-2xx response, throws `new Error(...)`. Per house rule 3, client code that calls the engine with `fetch` directly must surface errors as `ApiError` (with status, code, and message from the `{ error: { code, message, details } }` body) so pages can decide what to show. Throwing a plain `Error` means the findings panel will show a generic message and lose the server's status and error code. While a CSV download is a legitimate direct-`fetch` use (the response is a blob, not JSON), the error path should still throw `ApiError` with the status and, when the body is JSON, the code and message.

findings.title: Blob URL revoked immediately after click may race the download
findings.rationale: The click handler creates a blob URL, clicks the anchor, then immediately calls URL.revokeObjectURL(url). In some browsers the download may not have started reading the blob by the time the URL is revoked, causing a failed download. The standard pattern is to revoke in a setTimeout or after the download completes.

findings.title: CSV injection via unescaped cell values
findings.rationale: The new CSV export downloads a file that will be opened in spreadsheet applications. If the server-side CSV generation (not shown in this diff, but implied by the new endpoint) does not escape cell values that begin with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@`, a finding's title or description could inject a formula (e.g., `=HYPERLINK(...)`, `=cmd|...`). The client blindly trusts the blob and triggers a download. This is a real injection risk when the CSV is opened by a stakeholder. The PR description and diff do not show any escaping on the server side, and the client has no sanitization.

findings.title: Error path throws plain Error, losing ApiError contract
findings.rationale: The new `downloadFindingsCsv` uses a raw `fetch` and, on non-2xx, throws `new Error(...)`. Per the house rules (rule 3), client code that calls the engine with `fetch` directly must throw `ApiError` (or return the error body as data) so the UI can surface the server's `code`, `message`, and `details`. Here, a 404/500 from the new endpoint will surface as a generic 'Export failed: 404 Not Found' with no structured error, and the `FindingsPanel` has no try/catch to handle it — the error will propagate uncaught, potentially breaking the panel's render. This is a contract violation for the new endpoint's error path.

findings.title: Object URL not revoked on error path
findings.rationale: `URL.revokeObjectURL(url)` is called immediately after `a.click()`. In some browsers, the download may not have started by the time `revokeObjectURL` runs, causing the download to fail intermittently. The standard pattern is to revoke in a `setTimeout` or after the click event has been processed. This is a minor reliability issue, not a security defect.

findings.title: New `needs_discussion` verdict is not handled in the reducer's switch, so a PR that uses it throws at runtime
findings.rationale: The diff adds `needs_discussion` to the `VERDICT_RANK` map, but the `reduceVerdicts` function (which the diff does not touch) switches on the verdict string and has no `needs_discussion` case. When a PR's worst verdict is `needs_discussion`, the switch falls through to its default and throws. The PR description explicitly says agents will start returning this verdict, so this is not a dead path — it is the primary use case. The caller that breaks is the map-reduce reducer: any PR that contains a `needs_discussion` finding now fails at reduce time instead of producing a verdict. The compatible alternative is to add a `case 'needs_discussion':` to the switch in `reduceVerdicts` that returns the verdict (or falls through to the `comment`/`request_changes` handling as appropriate) in the same PR that adds the enum value.

findings.title: New enum value may break client code that exhaustively switches on Verdict
findings.rationale: The reducer's `VERDICT_RANK` is typed as `Record<string, number>`, so adding `needs_discussion: 2` compiles without forcing any other code that reads a `Verdict` to handle the new value. Any client or caller that deserializes a `Verdict` from the server and switches exhaustively over the previous three values (`request_changes`, `approve`, `comment`) will hit an unhandled case at runtime when the server returns `needs_discussion`. This is a silent behavior change for those callers: they keep working today, but the new value narrows what they can rely on. The compatible alternative is to ship the new value behind a feature flag, or to add a tolerant parse on the client (e.g. map unknown verdicts to `comment`) for one release so existing callers degrade gracefully.
